name: First Principles Thinking
oneSentence: Break a problem down to what you know is true, then rebuild from there.
definition: Reasoning from foundational truths rather than by analogy to how things are already done. Descartes resolved to doubt everything he could and rebuild only on what survived the doubting. The move is to strip a problem back to the things you can actually defend, then reason forward from those alone.

chains: inherited assumption
unexamined constraint
only incremental improvement
stripped to fundamentals
constraints tested
solutions convention was hiding

misconception: "It means ignoring what everyone else does." It does not require discarding convention. It requires knowing which parts of it are load-bearing. Most conventions encode a real constraint; the work is separating those from the ones that merely persist.
nearestNeighbour: CHESTERTON'S FENCE. That one warns you not to remove a convention until you understand why it exists. This one is the method for examining it. They pull in opposite directions and are strongest used together.
discriminateScenario: A caterer prices every job at twice her ingredient cost, because that is what her old employer did. When a large order loses money she sits down and works out what actually drives her costs, and finds that labour, not ingredients, is the thing her pricing should have been tracking all along.
praxisExercise:
STRIP IT DOWN

1. Name one rule you follow in your work.
2. Write down why you believe it is true.
3. For each reason ask: do I know this, or did I inherit it?
4. Keep only what you can defend, and rebuild the rule from those parts.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I catch myself saying this is how it is done, I will write down what I actually know to be true before going further."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Inversion
origin: Carl Jacobi, popularised by Charlie Munger
oneSentence: Solve a problem backwards by asking what would guarantee failure.
definition: Rather than asking how to succeed, you ask how you would reliably fail, then remove those conditions. Attributed to the mathematician Carl Jacobi, who advised inverting difficult problems, and made a standing habit of thought by Charlie Munger.

chains: forward question
vague aspirational answers
nothing to act on
inverted question
concrete failure conditions
specific behaviours to remove

misconception: "Inversion is just negative thinking." It is not pessimism. Failure conditions are simply easier to name precisely than success conditions, which is why inverting produces a list you can act on where the forward question produces platitudes.
nearestNeighbour: PREMORTEM. That one imagines a particular project has already failed and asks why. This is the general move of flipping any question on its head; the premortem is one applied instance of it.
discriminateScenario: Tom wants to write a book and keeps making plans that go nowhere. A friend asks him instead to list everything he could do to make sure he never finishes it. He names four things straight away, realises he is already doing three of them, and stops one that week.
praxisExercise:
FAILURE AUDIT

1. Choose one goal you currently care about.
2. Ask: how could I guarantee failure here?
3. List five behaviours that would make failure likely.
4. Mark the ones you are already doing.
5. Remove one of them this week.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I set a goal, I will write the five ways I could guarantee failure before I write any plan."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Principle of Charity
oneSentence: Interpreting what someone said in its strongest reasonable sense.
definition: A principle of interpretation holding that when a statement admits of several readings, you should engage the one that is most coherent and most likely to be meant. It is not generosity for its own sake. A weak reading of an argument tells you nothing about whether the argument is any good, so charity is a condition of learning anything from disagreement.

chains: you take the weakest available reading
you refute something nobody argued
you learn nothing and they do not change
you take the strongest reading
you engage the real claim
either you are changed or they are

misconception: "Being charitable means agreeing more, or being soft on bad arguments." It makes criticism harder to escape, not softer. Refuting the strongest version is a far more serious challenge than refuting a sloppy one, and the person cannot reply that you misunderstood them.
nearestNeighbour: STEELMANNING. That goes a step further and improves the argument beyond what was actually said, constructing the best possible case. Charity stays within what the person plausibly meant. One is accurate interpretation, the other is active reconstruction.
discriminateScenario: In a thread about remote work, someone writes that offices help junior staff. A reply treats this as a claim that everyone must return five days a week, and knocks it down easily. The original poster never meant that, and the exchange ends with both sides more certain than before.
praxisExercise:
THE BEST READING

1. Find something you disagreed with this week, in writing.
2. Write the reading of it you reacted to.
3. Write the strongest reading it could bear.
4. Decide whether your objection still holds against the second one.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I am about to disagree in writing, I will write the strongest version of their point first and check my objection against that."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Steelmanning
origin: Attributed to Daniel Dennett and others
oneSentence: Building the strongest version of an argument before you take it apart.
definition: A practice of constructing the best case for a position, including improvements its actual defenders have not made, and then responding to that. Where charity asks you to read fairly, steelmanning asks you to build. Its purpose is partly honesty and partly self interest, because an objection that only defeats a weak version has told you nothing about whether you are right.

chains: you argue against what was said
any weakness in their phrasing does your work for you
your own position is never tested
you argue against the strongest possible version
their phrasing is no longer the weak point
you find out whether you are actually right

misconception: "Steelmanning is a debate tactic for looking fair minded." If it is performed rather than done, it is worthless. The point is private, not social: you build the strong version in order to find out whether your own view survives it, and sometimes it does not.
nearestNeighbour: PRINCIPLE OF CHARITY. That asks you to interpret what was said in its strongest reasonable sense, staying within what the person meant. This goes beyond them, improving the argument past anything they said. Charity is about accuracy, this is about construction.
discriminateScenario: Before writing a piece arguing against a popular productivity method, Nadia spends an afternoon writing the best case for it she can manage. Two of her four objections do not survive the exercise. The piece she eventually publishes makes the remaining two, and is far harder to dismiss.
praxisExercise:
BUILD IT FIRST

1. Take a position you argue against.
2. Write the best case for it you can, including points its defenders usually miss.
3. Show it to someone who holds that view and ask what you left out.
4. Now write your objection, against that version.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I plan to argue against something publicly, I will write its strongest case first and check which of my objections survive."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Straw Man Fallacy
oneSentence: Refuting a distorted version of an argument instead of the real one.
definition: An error of reasoning in which a position is restated in a weakened or exaggerated form, and the weakened form is then defeated. The appearance of victory comes from the substitution, not from the argument. It is often unintentional, since the distorted version is usually the one that felt easiest to answer.

chains: real claim is hard to answer
a simpler version comes to mind
the simpler version is attacked
the original claim stands untouched

misconception: "A straw man is just any unfair characterisation of someone's view." Unfairness alone is not enough. The error is specifically substituting a weaker claim and then treating its defeat as a defeat of the original. Describing someone's view rudely but accurately is not this.
nearestNeighbour: MOTTE AND BAILEY. That is the mirror image, where a speaker defends a modest claim and then behaves as though a far bolder one had been established. One distorts the opponent's position downward, the other shifts one's own position back and forth.
discriminateScenario: A councillor proposes reducing the speed limit on two residential streets. At the public meeting a resident stands up to say that banning cars from the town centre would destroy local business, and sits down to applause. The speed limit proposal is never discussed.
praxisExercise:
FIND THE SUBSTITUTION

1. Recall an argument you felt you won easily.
2. Write what you argued against.
3. Write what they actually claimed, in their words if you have them.
4. If the two differ, your win was against something you built.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When an opposing argument feels easy to defeat, I will check their actual words before replying."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Ladder of Inference
oneSentence: We climb from what happened to what we conclude in steps we never notice taking.
definition: A description of the ascent from observation to action. You start with everything available, select part of it, add meaning drawn from your own experience, form an assumption, reach a conclusion, adopt a belief and act. The climb is fast and feels like a single act of perception, and the belief at the top then shapes what you select next time.

chains: everything observable
you select part of it
you add meaning from experience
you form an assumption
you conclude
you act
the belief shapes what you select next time

misconception: "It means your conclusions are wrong." The ladder is how all thinking works and nobody can avoid climbing it. The useful move is not to stop, it is to be able to say which rung you are standing on, and to climb back down to what was actually observable when someone sees it differently.
nearestNeighbour: CONFIRMATION BIAS. That is the tendency to seek and favour evidence fitting what you already believe. This describes the whole ascent from observation to action, of which that bias distorts one step, the selecting.
discriminateScenario: A manager notices one person is quiet in meetings, decides they are disengaged, stops asking for their opinion, and six months later has a year of evidence that they contribute nothing. Every step along the way felt like observation. Only the very first one was.
praxisExercise:
CLIMB BACK DOWN

1. Take a conclusion you hold about a person or a situation.
2. Write what you actually observed, with no interpretation in it at all.
3. Write what you selected from that, and what you added.
4. Ask whether a different reasonable person could have climbed somewhere else.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I find myself certain about someone's motives, I will write down what I actually saw before I act on it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Double Loop Learning
oneSentence: Fixing the error is one loop. Questioning the goal that produced it is the second.
definition: A distinction between two kinds of correction. Single loop learning adjusts actions to hit an existing target. Double loop learning puts the target itself, and the assumptions behind it, up for revision. Argyris found organisations overwhelmingly do the first, because the second requires examining commitments people would rather leave alone.

chains: result falls short
you adjust your actions
the aim behind it is never examined
the same kind of error returns wearing different clothes
result falls short
you ask whether the aim was right
the assumption that produced the error changes

misconception: "Double loop learning means reflecting more." Reflecting on how to do the thing better is still the first loop, however deep it goes. The second loop only begins when the goal, the measure or the governing assumption is itself available for revision, which is uncomfortable in a way that ordinary reflection is not.
nearestNeighbour: GOODHART'S LAW. That describes what happens when a measure becomes a target and stops measuring anything useful. This is the wider move of putting the target itself in question, and Goodhart is one of the reasons you might need to.
discriminateScenario: A charity's email open rates fall, so they test new subject lines for a year and claw back a few points. Nobody asks whether email is still how their supporters want to hear from them, because improving the number was the brief from the beginning.
praxisExercise:
QUESTION THE TARGET

1. Name something you are currently trying to improve.
2. Write the measure you are improving it against.
3. Ask who chose that measure, and what it was standing in for.
4. Write what you would do differently if the measure were wrong.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I have been trying to improve a number for more than a quarter, I will ask what it was standing in for."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Cynefin Framework
oneSentence: Different kinds of problem need different kinds of response, and the first job is telling which kind you have.
definition: A way of placing a situation before deciding how to act on it. Clear situations have an obvious right answer. Complicated ones have a right answer an expert can find. Complex ones have no answer available in advance, only patterns that appear once you act. Chaotic ones require acting first to establish any stability at all.

chains: one way of deciding is applied everywhere
it fits some situations and fails in others
the failures are read as poor execution
the situation is placed first
each kind gets the response that suits it
established practice is used only where established practice exists

misconception: "It sorts problems by how hard they are." Difficulty is not the distinction. A complicated problem can be extremely hard and still have a correct answer waiting for the right expert. A complex one can be simple to describe and have no answer available in advance at all, which is a different situation requiring a different move.
nearestNeighbour: FIRST PRINCIPLES THINKING. That is a method for stripping a problem back to what you know is true, and it suits situations where an answer exists to be found. This is the prior question of whether the situation in front of you is that kind at all.
discriminateScenario: A hospital rolls out a checklist that cut infections dramatically in one unit. In a second unit it changes nothing. In a third it makes handovers worse. The checklist was never wrong. It was answering a question only the first unit was actually asking.
praxisExercise:
PLACE IT FIRST

1. Take a problem you are stuck on.
2. Ask whether there is a known right answer, an answer an expert could find, or no answer available yet.
3. If there is no answer available yet, name one small safe thing you could try to learn from.
4. Do that rather than planning further.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When a plan keeps failing in execution, I will ask whether the situation has a knowable answer before planning again."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Via Negativa
origin: Ancient, popularised by Nassim Nicholas Taleb
oneSentence: You often improve something faster by removing what harms it than by adding what helps.
definition: A principle holding that subtraction is more reliable than addition. Its root is theological, defining the divine by what it is not, and it carries into practical matters as a claim about knowledge: we know what damages a system with far greater confidence than we know what improves it, so acting on the first is the better bet.

chains: improvement sought by adding
each addition brings effects of its own
the system grows more complicated and the original problem persists
improvement sought by removing
what is gone cannot misbehave
the change is more reliable than anything you could have added

misconception: "It means do less." It is not minimalism and it is not about effort. It is a claim about where reliable knowledge sits. Harm is easier to identify than benefit, so removing a known harm is a safer bet than adding a supposed good, and that holds whether you end up busier or not.
nearestNeighbour: INVERSION. That flips a question to ask what would guarantee failure, and it is a move you make while thinking. This is a claim about which kind of action is more trustworthy once you have an answer, and it favours removal over addition.
discriminateScenario: Asked how to sleep better, a man has already bought a tracker, a weighted blanket and three supplements. His doctor asks what time he stops drinking coffee. Nothing he had added was useless. The thing that was actually hurting him had never been on the list.
praxisExercise:
SUBTRACT ONE THING

1. Name something you are trying to improve.
2. List everything you have added in order to improve it.
3. Now list what might be harming it, however small.
4. Remove one item from the second list this week, and add nothing.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I want to improve something, I will look for one thing to remove before I add anything."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Sunk-Cost Fallacy
oneSentence: Carrying on with something because of what you already spent on it.
definition: A sunk cost is a cost already paid that cannot be recovered. The fallacy is letting it influence a decision about the future. Rationally, only the costs and benefits still ahead of you should count; in practice, what has already gone in exerts a strong pull toward continuing.

chains: resources already committed
continuing feels like recovering them
quitting feels like admitting waste
the decision is made on the past rather than the future

misconception: "It means you should quit things easily." It does not. Plenty of commitments are worth continuing on their own merits. The fallacy is specifically about using past expenditure as the reason, rather than whether the thing is still worth doing from here.
nearestNeighbour: LOSS AVERSION. That one is the general tendency to feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains. Sunk cost is a specific decision error that loss aversion helps explain. You can be loss averse without committing the fallacy, and the fallacy also draws on a reluctance to look inconsistent.
discriminateScenario: Elena is two years into a qualification she no longer wants, in a field she has decided against. Every time she considers stopping, she thinks about the fees and the evenings already spent. She signs up for another year, and cannot say what the qualification will actually get her.
praxisExercise:
THE FRESH START TEST

1. Name a commitment you are unsure about.
2. Ask: if I were arriving at this today, with none of the history, would I choose it?
3. If no, write what is actually keeping you in it.
4. Separate the reasons that look forward from the ones that look back.

COMMITMENT (if-then):
"When I notice I am justifying something by what I have already put in, I will ask what I would choose if I were starting from today."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Eisenhower Matrix
origin: Attributed to Dwight D. Eisenhower, set out by Stephen Covey
oneSentence: Sort what you have to do by urgent and important, and most of what feels pressing turns out to be neither.
definition: A sorting device that places every task on two axes, how urgent it is and how important it is. The four resulting groups get different treatment: important and urgent is done now, important and not urgent is scheduled, urgent and not important is declined or handed on, and neither is dropped.

chains: urgency is felt, importance is not
attention goes to whatever is loudest
important work is never started
both axes are marked
the urgent and unimportant becomes visible
it can be refused

misconception: "It is a to do list with four boxes." Sorting is not the point, and the matrix does nothing if you then work through all four groups anyway. Its whole function is to make the urgent but unimportant group visible so that you decline it, which is the one group most people never act on.
nearestNeighbour: OPPORTUNITY COST. That is about what you give up by choosing one thing over another, and it applies to any choice at all. This is a specific sorting device for time, and its work is done by the axis of importance rather than by comparing alternatives.
discriminateScenario: Every week Omar clears his inbox, answers each message the day it arrives, and leaves at seven feeling productive. The strategy document he has been meaning to write has not moved in four months. Nothing he did was wasted, and none of it was the thing that mattered most.
praxisExercise:
THE QUADRANT AUDIT

1. List everything you did yesterday, in half hour blocks.
2. Mark each one urgent or not, and important or not.
3. Add up the time that went to urgent and not important.
4. Pick one recurring item from that group and decide who else could hold it, or what happens if nobody does.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When something arrives marked urgent, I will ask whether it is important before I touch it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Regret Minimisation Framework
oneSentence: Choose by imagining yourself at eighty, looking back on whether you did it.
definition: A way of reframing a hard choice by projecting yourself to the end of your life and asking which option you would regret not taking. Bezos describes using it to decide whether to leave a secure job, on the grounds that the things people regret at eighty are rarely the risks they took.

chains: decision made from where you stand
the near term costs loom largest
you optimise to avoid discomfort now
decision made from age eighty
the near term costs shrink and the things not done grow
you optimise for what will still matter

misconception: "It means always take the bold option." It is not a bias toward risk. Plenty of choices look equally fine from eighty, and the framework says nothing about those. It only separates decisions where one option will still sting decades later from ones where it will not.
nearestNeighbour: PREMORTEM. That imagines a particular plan has already failed and works backwards to find the risks, so you can prevent them. This imagines a whole life rather than one project, and it weighs the things you did not do rather than the ways a plan could go wrong.
discriminateScenario: Ines has been offered a place on an expedition that would mean leaving a job she is comfortable in. She spends a week listing the risks. Then she asks what the version of her at eighty would say about it, and finds that the job does not appear anywhere in the answer.
praxisExercise:
THE VIEW FROM EIGHTY

1. Write the decision you are avoiding, in one line.
2. Picture yourself at eighty, looking back, and write what that person says about each option.
3. Note which option only looks frightening from where you are standing now.
4. Name the smallest step toward it you could take this month.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When a decision has been sitting unmade for more than a week, I will write what I would say about it at eighty before deciding."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: One-Way and Two-Way Doors
oneSentence: Decisions you can reverse deserve far less deliberation than ones you cannot.
definition: A way of sorting decisions by whether they can be undone. A two way door can be walked back through at modest cost, so it should be made quickly and corrected if wrong. A one way door cannot, so it deserves slow and careful treatment. The claim is that most decisions are the first kind and are treated as though they were the second.

chains: every decision gets the same process
reversible ones are deliberated as heavily as permanent ones
everything slows and the permanent ones are still rushed
doors are sorted first
reversible ones are made quickly and corrected
care is spent where it cannot be undone

misconception: "It means move fast on everything." The framework is as much about slowing down as speeding up. If most decisions are reversible and over deliberated, the small number that are not should be getting far more care than they currently receive, and usually they are not.
nearestNeighbour: OPTIONALITY. That is about deliberately keeping future choices open, and it is a position you hold over time. This is a judgement you make once about the decision in front of you, by asking what it would cost to walk it back.
discriminateScenario: A team spends six weeks and four meetings choosing which project tool to adopt, a change they could undo in an afternoon. The same month they sign a three year lease on an office after a single visit, because the landlord needed an answer by Friday.
praxisExercise:
SORT THE DOORS

1. List the five decisions currently open in front of you.
2. For each, write what it would cost to reverse in six months.
3. Mark which are genuinely one way.
4. Make one of the reversible ones today, and give one of the one way ones a proper hearing.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When a decision is taking more than a week, I will first write what it would cost to undo."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Ten Ten Ten
oneSentence: Ask how you will feel about this in ten minutes, ten months and ten years.
definition: A device for holding a decision at three timescales at once. The ten minute answer captures the immediate feeling, the ten month answer captures the practical consequence, and the ten year answer captures whether it touches anything that lasts. Choices that look different across the three are the ones worth slowing down for.

chains: a choice is felt at one timescale only
immediate discomfort dominates
the decision serves the next hour
the same choice is held at three timescales
what only stings briefly separates from what compounds
the decision serves the longer view

misconception: "The ten year answer is the one that counts." All three horizons are meant to be weighed. Some things genuinely matter in ten minutes and not at all in ten years, and a device that always deferred to the longest view would have you ignore every immediate need you have.
nearestNeighbour: PRESENT BIAS. That is the documented tendency to overweight immediate rewards against future ones. This is a practical device for countering it in the moment, and it can be used by someone who has never heard of the bias.
discriminateScenario: Mid argument, Dan is about to say the thing that would end it in his favour. He stops and asks what it will look like at the end of the week, and then at the end of the year. The first answer is satisfying. The other two are not, and he says something else.
praxisExercise:
THREE HORIZONS

1. Take a decision you are sitting on.
2. Write how you will feel about it in ten minutes.
3. Then in ten months.
4. Then in ten years.
5. If the three answers disagree, write which one you were about to act on.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I am about to act on how I feel right now, I will write the ten month and ten year answers first."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Circle of Competence
oneSentence: Know where the edge of what you actually understand sits, and treat crossing it as the decision.
definition: The area in which you have real working knowledge, bounded by an edge you can describe. Buffett's argument is that the size of the circle matters far less than knowing where its boundary runs, because confidence does not drop when you cross it and you will go on deciding as though you were still informed.

chains: the edge of your knowledge is unmarked
confidence stays level as you cross it
you decide outside it without noticing
the edge is marked in advance
crossing becomes a visible act
you either get help or decline

misconception: "It means staying in your lane and never learning anything new." The size of the circle is not the point and Buffett has been explicit that it can be widened. What matters is knowing where the edge runs, because a small circle with a well marked boundary is worth far more than a large one with a vague one.
nearestNeighbour: ILLUSION OF EXPLANATORY DEPTH. That is the finding that people believe they understand things in far more detail than they do, and it explains why the edge is hard to see from inside. This is the practical response, which is to mark the boundary before you are under pressure rather than after.
discriminateScenario: A founder who has built three software companies joins the board of a biotechnology firm, reasoning that business is business. Eighteen months in, he cannot say whether the central scientific claim in their pitch is plausible, and he has been voting on it the whole time.
praxisExercise:
DRAW THE EDGE

1. Name an area where people treat you as knowledgeable.
2. Write three questions in it you could answer confidently.
3. Write three you could not, and would have to guess at.
4. That second list is the edge. Say it out loud next time one of them comes up.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I am asked for a view outside what I can defend, I will say where my knowledge stops before I answer."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Barbell Strategy
oneSentence: Put most of what you have somewhere very safe and a little somewhere very risky, and nothing in the middle.
definition: A way of arranging exposure so that the worst case cannot ruin you and the best case can still pay. Most of your resources sit in something close to safe, a small portion goes into things with large potential upside, and the moderate middle is deliberately avoided. Taleb's argument is that the middle carries real downside without the upside that would justify it.

chains: resources sit in the moderate middle
a shock does real damage
and the upside was capped anyway
resources split between very safe and very risky
the safe side survives any shock
the small risky side can pay off without threatening the rest

misconception: "It is just a way of saying diversify." Diversification spreads bets across the middle and relies on them not failing together. This explicitly empties the middle, on the argument that moderate risk carries genuine downside while capping the sort of gain that makes carrying downside worthwhile.
nearestNeighbour: MARGIN OF SAFETY. That is about leaving enough room in a single decision that an error does not become a disaster. This is about the shape of a whole set of positions at once, and the safe half is what performs the function margin of safety performs inside one of them.
discriminateScenario: A writer keeps a steady part time contract that covers her rent and spends the rest of her week on a book with no advance and no guarantee. Colleagues keep telling her to find a better paid full time role in publishing. She points out that it would eat the time the book needs and still not be secure.
praxisExercise:
FIND YOUR MIDDLE

1. List where your time, money or reputation is currently committed.
2. Mark each one safe, moderate or genuinely risky.
3. Look at the moderate pile and ask what it is actually protecting you from.
4. Move one item out of the middle, in either direction.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I commit time or money to something moderate, I will ask whether it belongs at one end instead."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Ergodicity
origin: Statistical mechanics, applied to decisions by Ole Peters
oneSentence: What happens to a crowd on average is not what happens to one person over time.
definition: A system is ergodic when the average across many parallel instances matches the average of one instance followed through time. Many situations people face are not. Expected value is an average across the crowd, so where the two come apart it answers a question nobody asked, because you are living one life in sequence rather than many at once.

chains: the average across many players is positive
the bet looks worth taking
one player repeats it through time
a single ruinous outcome ends the sequence
the crowd average was never describing them

misconception: "It is a technical way of saying do not take big risks." The claim is sharper than caution. Expected value quietly assumes the two averages agree, and where they do not it is not slightly imprecise, it is answering a different question. The number can be correct and the advice drawn from it still wrong.
nearestNeighbour: EXPECTED VALUE. That computes the average payoff across every possible outcome weighted by its probability, which is an average across the crowd. This is the prior question of whether that average describes what happens to you in sequence, and where it does not, expected value is the wrong instrument rather than a rough one.
discriminateScenario: A hundred people each put a tenth of their savings into a scheme that usually returns well and occasionally takes everything. Across the hundred, in one round, the arithmetic looks excellent. One person doing it every year for twenty years almost certainly ends with nothing, and the arithmetic never said otherwise.
praxisExercise:
FOLLOW ONE PERSON THROUGH TIME

1. Take a decision you would repeat, or a risk you carry regularly.
2. Write what happens on average, across many people doing it once.
3. Now follow one person, yourself, doing it fifty times in sequence.
4. Ask whether any single outcome in that sequence ends the sequence. If one does, the average was never about you.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When something is justified to me by an average or an expected return, I will ask what happens to one person repeating it."
author: Claude draft, needs Lindsay review

name: Solomon’s Paradox
oneSentence: We reason more wisely about other people's problems than our own.
definition: Named for King Solomon, who counselled others wisely but governed his own household badly. Grossmann and Kross found that people reason about their own problems with measurably less wisdom, by which is meant acknowledging the limits of what they know, allowing for change, weighing other perspectives and seeking compromise, than about an identical problem belonging to someone else.

chains: my problem
high emotional proximity
narrowed perspective
poorer reasoning
someone else's problem
psychological distance
broader perspective
wiser reasoning

misconception: "People are just smarter about other people's lives." The effect is not about intelligence, and not about caring less. name: Attachment Theory

definition: Bowlby's claim was that the need for a reliable other is a biological system in its own right, not a by-product of hunger or sex. name: Secure Attachment

definition: The pattern is not an absence of need. It is a person who expects their need to be met and therefore states it plainly, early, and without strategy. a need can be stated directly rather than engineered
stating it usually works
the expectation is confirmed
distance and conflict stop reading as threat

name: Anxious Attachment

the other person withdraws from the pressure

nearestNeighbour: MICHELANGELO PHENOMENON. That is a partner eliciting the traits a person is deliberately reaching for, a directed process with a target the person has named. This is a general upward bias in perception with no particular aim attached to it.
discriminateScenario: Everyone agrees he is disorganised, including him. She describes him as someone whose mind is on bigger things, which is the same fact wearing better clothes. Asked whether he is disorganised she says yes, obviously. Asked what he is like she does not mention it. Five years in, he is noticeably better at it.

name: Differentiation of Self
oneSentence: Staying yourself while staying close, rather than choosing between the two.
definition: Bowen treated the family as a single emotional unit and asked how much of a person survives inside it. A poorly differentiated person has two options when the unit gets tense: fuse, meaning take on its anxiety as their own, or cut off, meaning leave and stay gone. Both are reactions to the same pressure and neither is a self. Differentiation is the third thing: holding your own position while remaining in contact with people who disagree with it and are upset about it.

chains: anxiety rises somewhere in the family
it travels through the unit and looks for somewhere to settle
a poorly differentiated person absorbs it as their own feeling or escapes contact entirely
either response keeps the unit’s anxiety in charge
holding a position while staying in the room is what interrupts it

misconception: "Differentiation means setting firm boundaries and not letting family affect you." Not being affected is cut off, which Bowen treated as the mirror image of fusion rather than the cure for it. The difficult version stays in contact and remains affected, and holds its own position anyway. Distance is the easy counterfeit.
nearestNeighbour: SEPARATION OF TASKS. That is an Adlerian rule for deciding whose problem a thing is, and it is a clean line you can draw in advance. This is a capacity rather than a rule, and it is specifically about staying close to people whose anxiety is pulling on you.
discriminateScenario: His mother cries on the phone about Christmas. He has two familiar moves: cancel his own plans and feel noble, or not take the call for three weeks. This year he says he is not coming, stays on the line while she is upset, asks about her week, and rings again on Sunday. It is the hardest thing he does that month.
praxisExercise:
STAY IN THE ROOM

1. Name one position you hold that someone in your family is upset about.
2. Write the two easy exits you usually take: give in, or go quiet and distant.
3. Next contact, hold the position and stay in contact. Ask them something about themselves.
4. Make the next contact yourself rather than waiting.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When family pressure rises, I will keep my position and keep the contact, rather than surrendering one to protect the other."

name: Perceived Partner Responsiveness
oneSentence: The belief that the other person understands you, values you and will act on it, which predicts more than almost anything else measured.
definition: Reis argued this single perception sits underneath most of what makes close relationships work. It has three parts: feeling understood, feeling valued, and feeling that the other will do something about your needs. What matters is the perception rather than the behaviour, which sounds like a weakness in the construct and is actually its point. A partner can be objectively helpful and not read as responsive, and the relationship tracks the reading.

chains: one person discloses something that matters
the other responds in a way that shows they took it in
the first reads understanding, valuing and willingness to act
disclosing becomes safe and happens more
each round supplies more material for the next

misconception: "Being supportive is about doing things for your partner." Doing the thing without showing you understood why it mattered often fails to register at all. The research finding is that the demonstration of understanding is doing the work, not the assistance, which is why unsolicited practical help can land as dismissal.
nearestNeighbour: BIDS FOR CONNECTION. Those are the small offers one person makes, counted from the side of whoever is reaching out. This is the reading the reacher takes from what came back, and it is the thing that actually predicts outcomes.
discriminateScenario: He tells her the presentation went badly. She immediately offers to review his slides for next time, which is generous and takes an hour. He thanks her and feels oddly worse. What he had wanted was for someone to say that sounds humiliating, and he cannot work out how to ask for that now without seeming ungrateful.

UNDERSTAND BEFORE YOU FIX

1. Recall the last time someone close brought you a problem.
2. Write what you offered. Then write whether you first said anything showing you grasped why it mattered to them.
3. Next time, say that sentence first and wait.
4. Only offer the fix if they ask for one.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When someone tells me something difficult, I will say what I understood about why it matters before I offer anything."

name: Bids for Connection
oneSentence: The small, deniable offers people make to be noticed, and the answer to which is the whole relationship.
definition: Gottman called them bids: reading something aloud, pointing at a bird, a hand on a shoulder, a question about nothing. Each one asks are you there, in a form small enough that refusal costs nothing. He described three responses. Turning toward, which answers it. Turning away, which misses it. Turning against, which punishes the asking. His observational work found couples who stayed together turned toward the large majority of bids, and couples who separated turned toward a minority of them.

chains: one person makes a small deniable offer
the other turns toward it, away from it, or against it
the asker learns what bidding costs here
the rate of bidding adjusts to match
the relationship thins or thickens one exchange at a time, below the level of anything either would call an event

misconception: "Relationships are won and lost in the big conversations." The big conversations are where the damage becomes visible, not where it is done. These exchanges are too small to remember and happen perhaps a hundred times a day, which is why their cumulative weight beats anything a single difficult discussion can do in either direction.
nearestNeighbour: PERCEIVED PARTNER RESPONSIVENESS. That is the standing belief that someone understands and values you, measured from the receiving side. These are the specific countable moments that build or erode it, measured from the side of whoever reached out.
discriminateScenario: He says huh, listen to this, and reads out two lines about a whale. She says mm without looking up. He does it again twenty minutes later with something about the weather and gets the same. By the evening he has stopped, and if asked she would say they had a perfectly nice day, which they did.

COUNT A DAY

1. For one day, notice every small offer someone close makes to you. Reading aloud, pointing, touching, asking nothing much.
2. Tally the ones you answered and the ones you did not.
3. Do not tell them you are counting.
4. The next day, answer every one, however trivial.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When someone close says something small to me, I will look up and answer it before finishing what I am doing."

name: Repair Attempts
oneSentence: The clumsy move someone makes mid argument to stop it getting worse, and whether the other person lets it work.
definition: A repair attempt is any effort to de escalate while a conflict is running: a joke, an apology for tone, a hand, let me start again, can we take ten minutes. Gottman’s observation was that happy and unhappy couples make them at similar rates. The difference is acceptance. In couples that lasted, a badly timed joke was received as the olive branch it was. In couples that did not, the same joke was read as evasion and the argument continued through it.

chains: conflict escalates past the point of usefulness
one person reaches for anything that might slow it
the attempt arrives clumsy, poorly timed or disguised as humour
the other either takes it as an offer or reads it as a dodge
the argument either ends there or runs until exhaustion

misconception: "Couples who argue less are doing better." Rate of conflict predicts very little. What predicts outcomes is whether either of them can stop one, and specifically whether a graceless attempt to stop one gets accepted. Learning to accept a bad repair is more useful than learning to make a good one.
nearestNeighbour: GOTTMAN’S FOUR HORSEMEN. Those are the four behaviours that make conflict corrosive, so they describe what goes wrong. This is the counter move, and the finding attached to it is about the listener rather than the speaker.
discriminateScenario: Forty minutes into it he says, in a bad voice, that at least they are getting their cardio in. It is not funny and it is not an apology. She has a choice in the next two seconds, and the whole evening turns on which way she goes, and she is too angry to notice she is choosing.
praxisExercise:
ACCEPT THE BAD ONE

1. Think of the last argument that ran too long.
2. Find the moment the other person tried to stop it. There almost always is one.
3. Write what you did with it.
4. Next time, take the next one offered, even if it is graceless and badly timed.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When someone tries to lighten or pause an argument, I will take it rather than pointing out that it was not good enough."

name: Gottman’s Four Horsemen
oneSentence: Four patterns in conflict that predict a relationship is in trouble.
definition: Gottman's observational work identified four communication patterns that reliably predict relationship breakdown: criticism, which attacks character rather than behaviour, contempt, which conveys superiority, defensiveness, which deflects responsibility, and stonewalling, which withdraws from the exchange altogether. Contempt was the strongest single predictor.

chains: complaint about behaviour
criticism of character
contempt
the partner defends
one of them withdraws
the cycle repeats with nothing addressed

misconception: "Gottman can predict divorce with over ninety per cent accuracy." That figure comes from models fitted to couples whose outcomes were already known, which is a much weaker thing than predicting an unknown future, and independent attempts to reproduce it have not matched it. The four behaviours are real and worth knowing. The accuracy claim attached to them is not settled.
nearestNeighbour: DEMAND WITHDRAW PATTERN. That is one specific cycle where one partner pursues and the other retreats, and it maps closely onto two of the four, criticism and stonewalling. The four horsemen are a wider set of markers rather than a single interactional loop.
discriminateScenario: Every time the finances come up, one of them starts with you never and the other starts with well you are the one who. Within four minutes one has stopped responding and is looking at their phone. They have had this exact exchange perhaps thirty times and have never once discussed the actual budget.
praxisExercise:
SPOT YOUR OWN

1. Recall your last difficult conversation with someone close.
2. Of the four, which one did you supply? Be specific about the sentence.
3. Write what the behaviour based version of that sentence would have been.
4. Use it next time the subject arises.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I catch myself starting a sentence with you always or you never, I will stop and name the specific behaviour instead."

name: Demand-Withdraw Pattern
oneSentence: One person presses for engagement, the other retreats from the pressing, and each move supplies the other’s reason.
definition: One partner pursues: raises the subject, asks for a response, escalates to be heard. The other withdraws: goes quiet, leaves the room, agrees to anything to end it. The structure is self feeding, because pursuit confirms that engagement is overwhelming and withdrawal confirms that pursuit is necessary. It is among the most replicated findings in couples research and predicts dissatisfaction across cultures. Which role each person takes is less stable than people assume and often swaps by topic.

chains: one raises something that matters
the other feels flooded and retreats
the retreat reads as not caring, so the first presses harder
harder pressing makes retreat more necessary
neither position is available to abandon, because each is a response to the other

misconception: "One of them is the problem, usually whoever is shouting." The pattern is a loop and has no author. The loudest person looks like the cause and is responding to silence, while the quietest looks reasonable and is producing the volume. Both halves have to move, and the one who moves first is usually whoever notices the shape.
nearestNeighbour: ATTACHMENT PROTEST BEHAVIOUR. That is one person’s moves when they feel the bond slipping, describable without reference to anyone else. This needs two people and exists only as a loop between them.
discriminateScenario: She brings up his mother’s visit. He says now is not a good time, three nights running. On the fourth she raises it at eleven at night with some heat in it, and he says this is exactly why he did not want to do this now, and walks to the kitchen. Both of them believe they have just been proved right.
praxisExercise:
NAME THE LOOP, NOT THE PERSON

1. Identify one subject where you and someone close reliably take these two positions.
2. Write which half you supply. Be honest; the quiet half counts.
3. Agree one rule in advance: a time limit, or a scheduled return, whichever your half needs.
4. Use it on that subject only, three times, before judging it.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I notice myself either pressing harder or going quiet, I will name the loop out loud instead of playing my half better."

name: Active Constructive Responding
oneSentence: How you answer someone’s good news predicts the relationship better than how you answer their bad news.
definition: Gable mapped four responses to a partner’s good news along two axes, active or passive and constructive or destructive. Active constructive is enthusiastic and curious, asking for more. Passive constructive is mild approval. Active destructive finds the problem with it. Passive destructive changes the subject. Her finding, which surprised the field, was that the response to good news predicted relationship wellbeing more strongly than the response to bad news did.

chains: one person brings good news, which is an offer of something they are pleased about
the response either amplifies it, flattens it, punctures it, or ignores it
the bringer learns what good news is worth here
they bring more or stop bringing it
shared pleasure is either a resource the relationship has or one it does not

misconception: "Being there for someone means showing up when things are bad." Being present in trouble is necessary and is not where the variance is, because most people manage it. Far more relationships are quietly thinned by the small puncturing of good news, which nobody logs as unkindness and which the research shows matters more.
nearestNeighbour: PERCEIVED PARTNER RESPONSIVENESS. That is the general belief that someone understands and values you, built from every kind of exchange. This is one narrow practice, defined only around good news, and it is the specific thing you can change on a Tuesday.
discriminateScenario: She says she has been asked to speak at the conference. He says that is great, then asks whether it is paid, and then whether it is the weekend of his brother’s thing. Every question is reasonable. By the end of it she is doing logistics and has not once said out loud that she is proud.
praxisExercise:
THE FIRST THIRTY SECONDS

1. Next time someone close brings you good news, say nothing practical for thirty seconds.
2. Ask two questions whose only purpose is to let them enjoy telling you.
3. Logistics and concerns can wait until later in the conversation.
4. Notice whether they tell you more next time.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When someone tells me good news, my first response will be a question that lets them keep talking about it, not a practical one."

name: Reciprocal Self Disclosure
origin: Irwin Altman and Dalmas Taylor, later Arthur Aron
oneSentence: Closeness is built by graded turns of telling, where each person goes slightly further than the last.
definition: Altman and Taylor described intimacy developing in layers, each disclosure licensing a slightly deeper one in return. Aron built the mechanism into a procedure: thirty six questions in escalating order, asked in turns by strangers, which reliably produced closeness ratings higher than small talk and in some pairs higher than ordinary friendships. The escalation and the reciprocity both matter. One person disclosing alone produces discomfort rather than closeness.

chains: one person says something slightly costly to say
the other matches it or goes marginally further
each round raises what is permissible
the risk taken is read as trust extended
closeness accumulates from the turn taking rather than from the content

misconception: "Opening up brings people closer." Only in turns. Unreciprocated disclosure is the most common way people mistake this, and it reliably produces the opposite: the listener feels burdened, the discloser feels exposed, and both pull back. The reciprocity is not politeness, it is the active ingredient.
nearestNeighbour: PERCEIVED PARTNER RESPONSIVENESS. That is about whether a disclosure is met with understanding, so it concerns the quality of the response. This is about the structure of the exchange itself, the taking of turns and the gradient, independent of how well any single response lands.
discriminateScenario: Forty minutes in, he has told her about his father’s drinking, the job he was pushed out of, and the thing he has never told anyone. She has said that must have been hard, three times, warmly. He walks home feeling strange and cannot name why, and will avoid her slightly for a fortnight.
praxisExercise:
MATCH THE DEPTH

1. Think of someone you want to be closer to.
2. Say one thing slightly costlier than you normally would. Then stop and wait.
3. If they match it, go one step further. If they do not, stay at that level.
4. Do not go three steps alone.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I notice I have disclosed more than the other person has, I will stop and let the turn pass rather than filling the silence."

name: Communal vs. Exchange Relationships
oneSentence: Two different rules for giving, and most trouble comes from two people running different ones.
definition: In an exchange relationship, benefits are tracked and reciprocity is expected on a comparable scale and timescale: colleagues, acquaintances, most commerce. In a communal relationship, benefits are given in response to need with no ledger, and introducing one is itself a violation. Clark and Mills showed the rules are so distinct that prompt repayment of a favour, which raises satisfaction in exchange relationships, lowers it in communal ones, because repaying marks the relationship as the other kind.

chains: a relationship is implicitly filed as communal or exchange
giving is then governed by need or by ledger
a move from the other rulebook reads as an insult rather than an error
the offended party rarely names what happened, because the rule was never stated
both conclude the other person is somehow wrong

misconception: "Fairness means keeping things even between people who are close." Evenness is the exchange rule, and applying it to a close relationship is what people experience as coldness. The communal rule is not generosity either; it is a different accounting in which need rather than balance determines who gives, and in which being owed is not a concept.
nearestNeighbour: COVERT CONTRACTS. Those are a specific failure in which someone runs a private ledger while presenting as communal, so the ledger is hidden deliberately. This describes the two legitimate rulebooks and the ordinary confusion of two people using different ones in good faith.
discriminateScenario: She drove him to the airport at five in the morning. He sends twenty pounds for the petrol that afternoon with a thumbs up. He thinks he has been considerate. She is annoyed and feels ridiculous for being annoyed, because he is right that petrol costs money, and neither of them raises it again.

name: Michelangelo Phenomenon
oneSentence: A partner who treats you as the person you are trying to become makes you more like them.
definition: The name comes from Michelangelo’s claim that the figure was already in the stone and his work was removal. Drigotas and Rusbult found partners do something similar: by perceiving and eliciting the traits a person is reaching for, they measurably move them toward their own ideal self, and movement toward it predicts satisfaction for both. The inverse exists too and is called disaffirmation, in which a partner perceives and elicits a version the person is trying to leave behind.

chains: one person has an ideal self they are moving toward
the partner perceives them as already carrying some of it
they behave toward that version and create situations calling for it
the person acts from it more often
the ideal self is approached, and both report higher satisfaction

misconception: "Loving someone means accepting them exactly as they are." Acceptance of who someone is and belief in who they are trying to become are not in competition, and the research suggests the second is doing more work than the first. What harms people is a partner sculpting toward their own preference rather than the person’s own stated ideal, which is a different thing and shows up as disaffirmation.
nearestNeighbour: SELF-EXPANSION MODEL. That is the passive version: being near someone different widens you with nobody intending it. This is directed, and it requires the partner to have noticed what you are actually aiming at rather than what they would prefer.
discriminateScenario: He has always described himself as not a details person. She keeps handing him the parts of their plans that need care, not as a test, because she appears to believe he is good at it. Two years in he is the one who books things properly, and he has quietly stopped using that phrase about himself.

ASK WHAT THEY ARE AIMING AT

1. Ask someone close what they are trying to become more of. Use their words, not yours.
2. Write the distance between that and how you usually treat them.
3. Create one situation this month that calls for the version they named.
4. Say nothing about why.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I catch myself describing someone close by a limitation, I will say the thing they are aiming at instead."

name: Covert Contracts
oneSentence: Giving in order to be owed, without telling the other person they have agreed to anything.
definition: A private agreement one party has signed and the other has not been shown. The giver does something generous, expects a specific return, and does not state it. Because it was never stated it cannot be refused, renegotiated or honoured on purpose. The predictable ending is resentment that feels entirely justified from inside, because a debt really was incurred, and bewildering from outside, because no debt was ever agreed.

chains: someone wants something they are unwilling to ask for
they give instead, treating the gift as a down payment
the terms stay unspoken, so the other cannot accept or decline them
the return does not come, because nobody knew it was due
resentment arrives feeling like evidence of being used

misconception: "This is just manipulation." Manipulation runs through terms the manipulator could state. The distinguishing feature here is that the person often cannot state them either, and experiences their own resentment as proof they were wronged rather than as the receipt for a contract nobody signed. Calling it manipulation ends the inquiry at the point it becomes useful.
nearestNeighbour: COMMUNAL VS. EXCHANGE RELATIONSHIPS. That describes two legitimate rulebooks for giving and the honest confusion of mixing them. This is specifically an exchange ledger disguised as communal giving, which is why the hiding is the defining part.
discriminateScenario: He has driven her to work every morning for five months and insisted it is no trouble, which he has meant. When she makes plans for Saturday without him, something in him goes cold and he cannot say why with a straight face. He has begun keeping a list, and the list has never once been read aloud.
praxisExercise:
READ THE CONTRACT OUT LOUD

1. Find one thing you do for someone that you privately feel should be noticed more.
2. Write the return you have been expecting. Be exact and unflattering.
3. Either ask for it directly, or keep doing the thing and give up the claim.
4. Those are the only two honest options.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I notice resentment about something I chose to give, I will either ask for what I actually wanted or drop the ledger."

name: Separation of Tasks
origin: Alfred Adler, popularised by Kishimi and Koga
oneSentence: Deciding whose task a thing is by asking who finally bears the outcome, and then staying out of the other person’s.
definition: The Adlerian test is simple: who ultimately lives with the result. Your child’s studying is their task, because they carry the consequence. Whether they resent you is also their task. Whether you nag is yours. The position is not indifference. Adler held that interfering in another person’s task is the main engine of interpersonal misery, and that help is legitimate when asked for and intrusion when not.

chains: ask who finally bears the outcome
that person owns the task
interference in their task produces resentment on both sides, because one is controlled and the other is responsible for something they cannot control
withdrawing from it returns the consequence to its owner
help becomes available on request rather than imposed

misconception: "This is a licence to stop caring what happens to people." Adler’s claim was the reverse: relationships are only possible once you stop trying to control outcomes that are not yours. The hard version keeps caring visibly and still does not interfere, which is considerably more demanding than either nagging or detaching.
nearestNeighbour: DIFFERENTIATION OF SELF. That is a capacity built over years for holding your own position inside an anxious family. This is a decision rule you can apply this afternoon to a specific situation, which makes it narrower and more immediately usable.
discriminateScenario: Her brother will not deal with the letters from the bank. She has rung on his behalf twice, which fixed nothing and made him furious. This time she tells him she thinks it is serious, says she will sit with him if he wants, and then does not ring the bank. It takes him five more weeks and he does it himself.

WHO BEARS IT

1. Name one situation where you are carrying something that belongs to someone else.
2. Write who finally lives with the outcome. That names the owner.
3. State your view once, offer help once, then stop.
4. Do not restate either.

"When I am about to intervene in something I will not bear the consequence of, I will say my view once, offer help once, and then leave it."

name: Lust, Attraction and Attachment Systems
oneSentence: Three systems that evolved for different jobs, run on different timescales, and need not point at the same person.
definition: Fisher proposed sex drive, which seeks partners generally, romantic attraction, which focuses energy on one, and attachment, which sustains a pair long enough to raise young. Her claim is that the three are partly independent, which explains being attached to one person while attracted to another, or desiring someone you have no interest in attaching to. The architecture is a useful organiser. The specific neurochemical assignments Fisher gave each system are not settled, and imaging work in this area has been criticised for small samples.

chains: three systems evolved for three different reproductive problems
each has its own triggers and its own timescale
they can activate together or separately
directed at one person they produce what people call being in love
directed at different people they produce the ordinary conflicts of adult life

misconception: "Love is one thing, so wanting someone else means something is wrong with your relationship." The framework’s most useful implication is that simultaneous attachment to one person and attraction to another is the predictable output of three systems rather than evidence of a failing bond. That is an explanation rather than a permission, and Fisher was explicit that what you do about it is not a biological question.
nearestNeighbour: TRIANGULAR THEORY OF LOVE. That is a psychological taxonomy of what love is made of, intimacy, passion and commitment, derived from how people describe their relationships. This is an evolutionary account of separate biological systems, and it makes claims about mechanism rather than about experience.
discriminateScenario: He has been with her for nine years and would be destroyed if she left. He also thinks about the woman from the Tuesday class more than he would say out loud, and feels no pull to do anything about it. He has decided this makes him a bad person, and has never considered that it might simply be ordinary.

name: Dependency Paradox
origin: John Bowlby, named by Levine and Heller
oneSentence: The more reliably someone can depend on another person, the more independently they act.
definition: Bowlby called it a secure base. A child with a dependable caregiver explores further from them, not closer. The counterintuitive part is that the exploration is caused by the dependability rather than limited by it. The adult version holds: people in reliably responsive relationships take more career risk, travel more, and recover faster from setbacks than people managing alone. Having somewhere to return to is what makes leaving cheap.

chains: one person is reliably responsive
the other stops spending attention on whether support will be there
that attention becomes available for everything else
they range further and risk more
returning costs nothing, so going out stays cheap

misconception: "Needing someone makes you weak, so independence has to be built alone." The evidence runs the other way. Forced self reliance produces vigilance rather than freedom, because the question of who would catch you stays permanently open. The independence people admire usually turns out to be sitting on top of one or two relationships nobody sees.
nearestNeighbour: SECURE ATTACHMENT. That describes a person and how they hold closeness. This describes a consequence, and specifically a counterintuitive one about autonomy, which is why it is worth separating from the pattern that produces it.
discriminateScenario: She takes the job in another country, which everyone reads as her being fearless. What actually happened is that he said he would come for a month at a time and she believed him without needing to check. The version of her who would have stayed is the version who had nobody to call at two in the morning.

name: Emotional Bank Account
oneSentence: Trust as a balance that small reliable acts pay into and that one withdrawal can overdraw.
definition: Covey’s metaphor: every interaction deposits or withdraws. Deposits are keeping small promises, remembering what matters to someone, apologising cleanly. Withdrawals are broken commitments, unkindness, taking someone for granted. The useful part is the asymmetry. A high balance means a mistake is absorbed as an exception. A low balance means the same mistake is read as the pattern finally showing itself, and the identical act lands as either forgivable or damning depending on the balance behind it.

chains: small acts accumulate as a balance of trust
the balance sets how any new act is interpreted
an identical mistake reads as an exception at a high balance and as confirmation at a low one
interpretation then changes the response
the response moves the balance again

misconception: "Trust is built by big gestures and broken by big betrayals." The accounting runs mostly on small change. Remembering a name, arriving when you said, replying to the dull message: the balance is built from items too small to be remembered individually, which is also why people cannot explain why they do or do not trust someone.
nearestNeighbour: BIDS FOR CONNECTION. Those are offers of contact and the finding attached to them is about whether they are answered. This is about accumulated trust and specifically about how a balance changes the reading of whatever happens next.
discriminateScenario: Two colleagues each forget the same meeting in the same week. One gets a message asking if everything is all right. The other gets copied into a note to the manager. Neither outcome is about the meeting, and anyone looking only at the week would see two identical events.

THE SMALLEST PROMISE

1. Pick one person whose balance with you is low or uncertain.
2. Make one small promise to them this week. Small enough that keeping it is certain.
3. Keep it exactly, on time, without mentioning that you did.
4. Repeat weekly for a month before expecting anything.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When I say I will do something small, I will treat it as the whole account rather than as a small thing."

name: Schema Chemistry
oneSentence: The pull toward the person whose behaviour confirms what you already believe about being loved.
definition: Young observed that the strongest attraction often runs toward someone whose patterns activate a person’s existing schema rather than contradict it. Someone who learned love is conditional finds withholding people compelling, and finds steady availability flat. The chemistry is real and is reporting familiarity rather than fit. Young’s clinical claim is that the intensity itself is diagnostic, and that the recognition people describe as knowing someone immediately is often recognition of a pattern rather than of a person.

a person appears whose behaviour matches that belief
the match registers as intensity and recognition rather than as familiarity
the relationship confirms the belief in operation
the belief is strengthened and the next pull is stronger

misconception: "If it feels this strong there must be something real there." Intensity measures fit with a template, not fit with a person, and Young’s point is that the most schema confirming partner produces the strongest pull. The corollary is the hard part: a healthier relationship often feels muted at the start, and that flatness gets read as absence of chemistry.
nearestNeighbour: LIMERENCE. That is the involuntary obsessive state of early infatuation, a condition with a course and a duration. This is about the selection that happened before it, and specifically why the pull went to this person rather than another.
discriminateScenario: Every person she has wanted badly has been slightly unavailable, and she has a theory about each one explaining why that case was different. The man who texts back promptly and says what he means she describes as lovely, and she does not think about him between meetings. She has noticed the pattern and has not yet let it change a decision.

LIST THE PATTERN

1. Write the three people you have wanted most. Beside each, one sentence on how they handled closeness.
2. Look for what the three share. It is usually obvious and unwelcome.
3. Write what belief about love that pattern keeps proving.
4. Keep the list. You will need it the next time something feels immediate.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When an attraction feels instant and certain, I will check it against my list before treating the intensity as information about them."

name: The Five Love Languages
oneSentence: The claim that each person has one primary way of receiving affection, and that mismatches explain unhappiness.
definition: Chapman, a pastoral counsellor, proposed five channels: words of affirmation, quality time, receiving gifts, acts of service and physical touch. Each person is said to have a primary one, and the prescription is to give in your partner’s rather than your own. The book has sold in the tens of millions. The empirical record is thin: studies find little support for discrete primary languages, no reliable improvement from matching, and the five category structure does not hold up well when tested.

chains: the framework proposes one dominant channel per person
affection given in another channel is said not to register
partners are told to identify and then speak the other’s language
the research finds no stable primary languages and no benefit from matching
what does hold is the ordinary point that people differ in what they notice

misconception: "Find out your partner’s love language and the mismatch resolves itself." Tests of exactly this have not supported it. People do not sort cleanly into one of five, most value most of them, and matching does not reliably improve satisfaction. The useful residue is much smaller than the framework: asking someone what makes them feel cared for, and believing the answer, which needs no taxonomy.
nearestNeighbour: PERCEIVED PARTNER RESPONSIVENESS. That is the well supported construct this framework gestures at: whether someone feels understood and valued. It makes no claim about discrete channels, and it is what the evidence actually points to.
discriminateScenario: They did the quiz on the sofa and he came out as acts of service, so for two months she did things rather than saying things. He appreciated it and still felt unseen. Nothing in the quiz covered the thing he had been missing, which was being asked about his day and having the answer remembered on Thursday.

name: The Five to One Ratio
oneSentence: The claim that stable couples produce roughly five positive exchanges for every negative one during conflict.
definition: From Gottman’s observational coding of couples in his laboratory: during conflict, couples who remained together showed around five positive behaviours to each negative one, while those who separated approached one to one. The underlying observation that positive exchanges must substantially outnumber negative ones is widely accepted. The specific number carries more weight in popular use than the data supports, having come from a modest sample of couples in a particular setting, and attempts to use it as a target rather than a description have no evidence behind them.

chains: negative exchanges in conflict carry more weight than positive ones
a surplus of positive behaviour is needed to offset them
couples who maintain a surplus absorb conflict without accumulating damage
couples near parity accumulate it
the balance rather than the frequency of conflict is what tracks outcomes

misconception: "Aim for five good things to every criticism and the relationship improves." The figure is a description of couples already doing well, not an instruction that produces the state. Manufacturing compliments to hit a quota is not what was measured, and the related claim of a universal positivity ratio in psychology was retracted after its mathematics was shown to be unsound.
nearestNeighbour: GOTTMAN’S FOUR HORSEMEN. Those are four specific corrosive behaviours, named and identifiable in a transcript. This is a quantitative balance across all behaviour during conflict, and its problem is the precision of the number rather than the behaviours it counts.
discriminateScenario: They have started keeping score, sincerely and with good intentions. He adds a compliment after each complaint and she has noticed the rhythm of it. The arithmetic is being satisfied and the warmth it was supposed to measure has quietly left the room, which neither of them can say without sounding ungrateful.

name: Attachment Injury
oneSentence: A specific moment where someone needed the other most and was not there, which keeps reappearing until it is addressed directly.
definition: Johnson identified a pattern in couples who could not progress in therapy: a single incident, often small to an outsider, where one partner reached for the other at a moment of real need and found nothing. A hospital waiting room. A funeral. A miscarriage. The incident is not a grievance to be resolved by apology for the facts. Until the hurt partner can say what it meant about whether they can count on the other, and be heard saying it, every subsequent conflict routes back through it.

chains: one partner reaches at a moment of acute need
the other is absent, dismissive or elsewhere
the event is encoded not as a failure of behaviour but as evidence about whether the bond holds
it becomes unavailable to ordinary repair
each later conflict reactivates it, so arguments about anything become arguments about that

misconception: "We have been over it, they apologised, they should let it go." Apology for the facts does not reach it, because the wound is not about the facts. What closes it is the hurt partner being able to say what the moment told them about being alone, and the other being able to hear that without defending the circumstances. That is a different conversation from the one most couples keep having.
nearestNeighbour: REPAIR ATTEMPTS. Those operate inside a live argument and work in seconds, de escalating something in progress. This is a single historical event that sits underneath many arguments, and it does not respond to in the moment repair at all.
discriminateScenario: Every argument about the washing up ends up at the night of the scan four years ago, and he cannot see how they got there. He has apologised for not leaving work that day perhaps thirty times. She accepts each apology and the subject returns, because what she needs to say about that afternoon has never once been the thing he apologises for.

THE ONE INCIDENT

1. Name the moment you keep returning to. One incident, one day.
2. Write what it told you about whether you could count on them. Not what they did.
3. Say that sentence to them, once, when nothing else is being argued about.
4. If you are the other person: do not explain the circumstances. Answer the sentence.

COMMITMENT (if then):
"When an argument lands on the same old incident again, I will stop arguing the facts of it and say what it told me instead."

name: Active Listening
oneSentence: Listening to understand the person rather than to prepare your reply.
definition: A practice in which the listener's whole attention goes to building an accurate picture of what the speaker means, and the speaker can see that happening. It involves not interrupting, not rehearsing a response while the other person talks, and checking your understanding out loud before responding to it. Rogers and Farson set it out as a working method rather than a personality trait.

chains: attention on your own reply
you hear only the parts you can answer
the speaker feels processed
attention on their meaning
you hear the whole thing
the speaker feels understood and says more

misconception: "Active listening means nodding and saying mm hmm." Those are signals, not the practice. A person can nod continuously while composing their rebuttal. The practice is the internal act of trying to build their meaning rather than your answer, and the signals only matter if that is actually happening.
nearestNeighbour: REFLECTIVE LISTENING. That is one technique inside this practice, where you say back what you understood. Active listening is the wider posture of attending to meaning first, which can be shown in many ways besides reflecting.
discriminateScenario: Priya's colleague starts describing a problem with the schedule. Twenty seconds in, Priya has the answer and is waiting for a pause to say it. She delivers a good solution. Her colleague thanks her, and does not mention the part he had not got to yet, which was the actual difficulty.
